human_tolerance.notes: 'can be found in urban areas, where it can become tame and will come to bird feeders' and 'The scrub jay even will eat peanuts off a human hand'; 'very common west of the southern Rocky Mountains', which is where Colorado Springs sits. light_max and flight_distance_m are judgement, not separately sourced numbers.

phases.name: nesting
phases.note: 'Nests are built low in trees or bushes, 1-10 m above the ground, primarily by the female, while the male guards her efforts.' The nest is 'sturdy, with an outside diameter of 33-58 cm, constructed on a platform of twigs with moss and dry grasses lined with fine roots and hair.'

phases.name: breeding
phases.note: 'Four to six eggs are laid from March through July, with some regional variations.' Eggs are pale green with irregular olive spots, or pale greyish-white to green with reddish-brown spots. 'The female incubates the eggs for about 16 days. The young leave the nest about 18 days after hatching.'

phases.name: caching
phases.note: 'Woodhouse's scrub jays, like many other corvids, exploit ephemeral surpluses by storing food in scattered caches within their territories. They rely on highly accurate and complex memories to recover the hidden caches, often after long periods of time.' Plant food - grains, nuts and berries - is weighted to winter in the Foraging section.

phases.name: territorial
phases.note: Caches are placed inside a defended territory and the birds defend them: 'To protect their caches from potential pilferers, food storing birds implement a number of strategies to reduce this risk of theft', including choosing sites out of sight of competitors, re-caching once alone, and 'they check first that no other jays are watching' before hiding their own acorns.

vocalizations.description: 'The call is described as "harsh and scratchy".' The source gives a single description of the voice, so it fills both the song and alarm slots of the shared program rather than two invented songs being split out of one adjective.

external.note: GBIF usage key, authorship and order from the GBIF Backbone Taxonomy; the iNaturalist taxa API matched taxon 506117 to "Woodhouse's Scrub-Jay"; ITIS TSN and NCBI taxon id from Wikidata (P815, P685). The English Wikipedia article title is "Woodhouse's scrub jay", without the hyphen.

common_names.note: The species is named for the American naturalist and explorer Samuel Washington Woodhouse; the source also warns that 'While many refer to scrub jays as "blue jays", the blue jay is a different species of bird entirely'.

range.note: 'native to western North America, ranging from southeastern Oregon and southern Idaho to central Mexico', plus 'very common west of the southern Rocky Mountains'. The state list is an approximation of that description and is not exhaustive. No elevation range is given, so elevation_m is omitted.

traits.note: Covers the structural traits (body plan, limb count, thermoregulation, skin, flight, respiration, metamorphosis, perching) and locomotion modes: a perching corvid that forages in scrub, brush and tree canopy, hops and walks on the ground, and flies between territories and roosts.

traits.nest_type.note: Nesting section: nests are 'built low in trees or bushes, 1-10 m above the ground... sturdy, with an outside diameter of 33-58 cm, constructed on a platform of twigs' - a twig platform, so Platform rather than Cup.

traits.size_class.note: From mass_kg (~0.08 kg); the validator's size-class bands place this in the Small band.

traits.mass_kg.note: 'about 80 g (2.8 oz) in weight' - a directly stated figure.

traits.mass_range_kg.note: HONEST GAP: the source gives a single point value of about 80 g and no range. The 70-90 g band is authored to bracket it and is flagged here rather than presented as sourced; no published weight range for this taxon was found in the CC0/CC BY sources used.

traits.length_m.note: Midpoint of the stated 27-31 cm including the tail.

traits.wingspan_m.note: 'a 39 cm (15 in) wingspan' - a directly stated single figure, not a midpoint.

traits.lifespan_y.note: 'The life span of wild Woodhouse's scrub jays is approximately 9 years.'

traits.diet.note: Foraging section: 'They feed on small animals, such as frogs and lizards, eggs and young of other birds, insects, and (particularly in winter) grains, nuts, and berries.' Shares follow that ordering; the plant third is divided into seed, mast and fruit as judgement, and the winter emphasis on plant food is carried on the mast resource's months rather than in the diet shares.

traits.social.note: 'Woodhouse's scrub jays usually forage in pairs, family groups, or small non-kin groups, outside of the breeding season', with the male guarding the female while she builds the nest - a pair-centred breeding unit with a family group afterwards.

traits.activity_pattern.note: Judgement: a diurnal corvid; the source describes daytime feeder visits, nest building by daylight and cache watching, without labelling the pattern.

traits.defense.note: 'They can be aggressive towards other birds, for example, they have been known to steal hoarded acorns from Acorn Woodpecker granary trees', they rob Clark's nutcracker stores, and they watch for and outwit pilfering conspecifics. The schema's enum offers Mob for the dominant response to a competitor.

traits.wariness.note: 'can be found in urban areas, where it can become tame and will come to bird feeders' and 'The scrub jay even will eat peanuts off a human hand' - about as tame as a wild bird gets, so the lowest end of the scale was authored.

habitat.note: Covers shelter_tag and habitat.resources. Prey, seed, mast and fruit tags come from the Foraging and Food storing sections; nest_platform and perch from the Nesting section and from territorial life in shrubs and low trees. Weights are judgement, not separately sourced percentages.

habitat.use.note: Judgement from the Habitat, Foraging and Food storing sections: the bird works in low scrub and open woodland, 'sometimes land[s] on the backs of mule deer to eat ticks', and stores food in scattered caches within its territory, which implies much time in trees and shrubs with ground foraging for insects and vertebrates. No numeric split is given in the source.

habitat.human_tolerance.note: Lead and Food storing sections, quoted in the field: 'can be found in urban areas, where it can become tame and will come to bird feeders' and 'The scrub jay even will eat peanuts off a human hand'. light_max and flight_distance_m are judgement, not separately sourced numbers.

seasonal.strategy.note: 'Woodhouse's scrub jay is nonmigratory', with year-round territory defence and caching, so ActiveYearRound was used.

seasonal.phases.note: Nest building and laying 'from March through July' with the quoted incubation and nestling figures, autumn cache-filling with plant food weighted to winter, and year-round territoriality over the caches. Day-of-month boundaries follow the source's 'March through July'; the caching window is judgement, aligned to the autumn surplus the Food storing section describes. The nesting and breeding phases are tagged US-CO because the locale that prompted this record is in Colorado, inside the 'very common west of the southern Rocky Mountains' range; the source's dates are continental.

seasonal.life_stages.note: Nesting section: 'The chicks start off fully gray. The older they get, the more they turn blue. On their heads, chicks tend to have a red crest that resembles a comb... The chick will lose its crest at day seven', and 'the young leave the nest about 18 days after hatching.' No sourced juvenile-plumage duration was found, so duration_days is unset and the juvenile scale is judgement.

vocalizations.scratchy_call.note: Description section: 'The call is described as "harsh and scratchy".' That is the only description of the voice in the source, so it fills both the song and alarm slots of the shared perching-songbird program; the id carries an underscore because the validator restricts call ids to lowercase letters, digits and underscores.

look.note: Description section: 'The species has a blue head, wings, and tail; a gray-brown back; and grayish underparts. The throat is whitish with a partial blue breast band ("necklace")', and the call 'harsh and scratchy'. The palette maps blue onto head, wings and tail and grey-brown onto the body slot, with the greyish underparts on the breast; compared with the California scrub jay this taxon has 'a duller blue, darker gray underparts, a less distinct blue necklace, and a straighter bill', which the chosen colours reflect. Proportions are authored judgement from the 27-31 cm length and 39 cm wingspan.

behavior.note: Authored parameters for the shared perching-songbird program: food_tag is the invertebrate share, which the program uses for ground foraging; flee_m is low because the bird is famously tame; nest_m1/nest_m2 span the stated March-July nesting season.
